# The first hundred

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-04 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: The first hundred community members are recruited, not attracted. Hand-pick them, give them real influence and close the loop on every contribution. They become your testers, your references and your first distribution channel. This piece is about getting them: who to list, what to ask and how 30 names become 100. Its companion, [Find your first 100 people who actually care](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/), covers what to do once they are in the room.

## Key points

- A hundred is small enough to know by name and large enough to start sustaining itself.
- Recruit by hand from 30 named people; Paul Graham calls recruiting users manually the most common unscalable thing founders must do.
- Ask for judgment on a real decision, not attention.
- Close the loop in public. Research on online groups shows newcomers who get a response are far more likely to stay.
- A small core does most of the work in any community, so the first hundred should be chosen for contribution, not reach.

The first hundred is the foundation stage in our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/). It follows from the argument that [community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/): before anyone can do the job, someone has to be asked.

## Why a hundred

A hundred is small enough to know by name and large enough to generate a steady flow of feedback, referrals and public advocacy. It is also roughly the size at which a community can begin to sustain itself: members start answering each other's questions and bringing in people you would never have reached.

Below that, it is the founder's personal network. Above it, without the first hundred in place, it is usually an audience.

The composition matters more than the count because participation is unequal from the start. In a 2014 study of four digital health networks with 63,990 members, the most active 1% wrote 74.7% of posts and the next 9% wrote 24.0%. Jakob Nielsen's 90-9-1 analysis describes the same pattern across blogs, Wikipedia and product reviews. If one person in a hundred will do most of the work, the founder's job is to make sure that person is in the first hundred.

## The recruitment loop

| Step | What you do | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| List 30 names | Write down potential customers, respected builders, operators in your category and sharp critics | Forces specificity; you cannot recruit a category |
| Ask for judgment | "We're deciding between two approaches to X. Would you look at both and tell me which is wrong?" | Specific, flattering in the right way and easy to answer |
| Give the yeses a job | Early access, a test, a draft to tear apart, with an end date | Turns interest into a first contribution |
| Close the loop in public | "We changed this because Priya pointed out Y." | Shows input leads somewhere |
| Ask for the next name | "Who else should see this?" at the end of every exchange | How 30 becomes 100 without a campaign |

**List 30 names.** Pick people whose use of the product would teach you the most or whose endorsement would mean the most. Paul Graham's 2013 essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" put it bluntly: "The most common unscalable thing founders have to do at the start is to recruit users manually."

**Ask for judgment, not attention.** A request for an opinion on a live decision is easier to say yes to than a request to join something. It also tells you who thinks carefully, which is the trait you are recruiting for.

**Give the yeses a job.** Early access, a test, a draft to tear apart. Something with an end date, so saying yes is a small commitment.

**Close the loop in public where you can.** This is the step most teams skip and the one that turns a respondent into a member. The evidence for it is strong. Kraut and colleagues' study of Usenet newsgroups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day. By day 30, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still participating, against 12% of those who got no reply. A related CHI 2006 paper found 27% of posts received no response at all, and newcomers were less likely to get one than established members.

**Ask for the next name.** Each person who engages is asked who else should see it. This is the same mechanic as a good investor introduction or customer referral: give the person homework, do something visible with their answer, then ask for the next name. Run it once and it works for all three audiences.

> Give the person homework, do something visible with their answer, then ask for the next name.

## What to give them

**Access:** builds, roadmaps, the founder's time.

**Influence:** a real decision they shaped, and evidence they shaped it.

**Recognition:** named in changelogs, release notes, docs credits or onchain roles.

**Each other:** introduce members to one another. A community whose members know each other survives the founder getting busy.

What not to give them: vague promises of future token allocations, or anything you would regret seeing in a screenshot.

Rejection is the hidden cost to avoid. Halfaker and colleagues' 2013 study of English Wikipedia found the number of active editors stopped growing in early 2007 and then declined, driven by falling retention of good-faith newcomers rather than veterans leaving. Those newcomers were more likely than earlier cohorts to have their first contributions reverted, often by automated tools. In a first hundred, every early contribution deserves a human response.

## Where to keep them

Somewhere small and owned. A private group, an email list, a feedback channel. The public server can come later. The first hundred need a room where they can be candid, and you need records you keep even if a platform changes its rules.

Record each person's source, first contribution and what changed because of it. That record is what makes the loop closable, and it is the start of the member-health review described in the companion piece on the [first 100 people who actually care](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/).

## Web3 and AI notes

For a web3 protocol, the first hundred should include people who actually use DeFi daily, not only holders. They will find the confusing parts of your app in minutes. Our piece on [community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) covers why wallet balance is the wrong recruiting filter.

For an AI product, include at least ten people who would pay for it. Enthusiasts give great feedback on features; buyers give great feedback on whether it is worth money. If the first hundred later become a source of introductions, the rules in [referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) apply on a smaller scale: register the introduction and credit the person who made it.

Illustrative example: 30 names to 100

Decision
:   A two-founder AI analytics start-up listed 30 people (eight prospective buyers, twelve practitioners, six builders of adjacent tools and four known critics) and asked each to judge two competing onboarding designs.

Reason and owner
:   The founders needed a decision within a month and had no community. One founder owned the list and every reply.

What changed
:   Nineteen replied. The team shipped the design most of them preferred, credited them by name in the release note and asked each for one more name. The group passed 100 people in about ten weeks.

Illustrative: a composite of early-stage patterns, not a single company; the figures show the shape of the loop, not a benchmark.

## The checklist

- 30 named people, written down.
- A real decision to ask them about.
- A small, owned space for the ones who say yes.
- Every contribution acknowledged in public or in the product.
- A "who else should see this?" at the end of every exchange.

## lowob takeaways

- **Recruit, do not attract.** A hundred is small enough to know by name and large enough to start sustaining itself.
- **Ask for judgment.** A real decision draws better people than a request to join.
- **Close the loop in public.** It is the step most teams skip and the one that turns a respondent into a member.
- **Include buyers.** For an AI product, include at least ten people who would pay for it.

## Common questions

### How do I get the first 100 members of a startup community?

List 30 names, ask them for judgment on a real decision, give those who say yes a job with an end date, close the loop in public, and ask each for the next name.

### Why do new community members stop participating?

Often because nobody responds. In one study of newsgroups, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still active after 30 days, against 12% of those who got none.

### What should I give early community members?

Access to builds, roadmaps and founder time; real influence with evidence of it; public recognition; and introductions to each other.

### Who should be in the first hundred users of a Web3 protocol?

People who actually use DeFi daily, not only holders, because they will find the confusing parts of your app in minutes.

## Sources and notes

- [Paul Graham, Do Things That Don't Scale](https://www.paulgraham.com/ds.htm), July 2013. Founder essay; examples drawn from Y Combinator companies.
- [Kraut, Wang, Butler, Joyce and Burke, Beyond Information: Developing the Relationship between the Individual and the Group in Online Communities](https://www.dhi.ac.uk/san/waysofbeing/data/communication-zangana-kraut-2008.pdf), manuscript dated 18 April 2008. Working paper; Usenet groups; behavioural measures only.
- [Arguello and colleagues, Talk to me: foundations for successful individual-group interactions in online communities, CHI 2006](https://dx.doi.org/10.1145%2F1124772.1124916), April 2006. Peer-reviewed; 6,172 messages from eight Usenet groups.
- [Halfaker, Geiger, Morgan and Riedl, The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System, summary on Wikimedia Meta](https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Research:The_Rise_and_Decline), 2013. Published in American Behavioral Scientist; English Wikipedia only.
- [van Mierlo, The 1% Rule in Four Digital Health Social Networks, Journal of Medical Internet Research](https://www.jmir.org/2014/2/e33/), 4 February 2014. Peer-reviewed; health networks, not commercial communities.
- [Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/), 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; ratios are a rule of thumb.
- The recruitment table, checklist and example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.
